newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - James Unruh resigns as Unisys chairman, CEO.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - James Unruh resigns as Unisys chairman, CEO.

text.p: James Unruh resigned Thursday as chairman and chief executive officer of Unisys Corp. after seven years at the helm of the struggling computer maker, which is now embarking on a search for a new CEO.

A spokesman said Unruh decided to resign of his own accord. With Unisys now reaching financial stability, it is the appropriate time for a new CEO to focus on the company's growth opportunities, he added.

"He thinks he has come to the end of the repositioning phase," said spokesman J. Peter Hynes. "Unisys is now moving into a growth phase ... Jim has been thinking about his future for several months and he made a decision that included it was the right time to make a change in terms of the company and from a personal point of view."

Unruh will step down as CEO once a successor is named and will remain as chairman until Unisys' next annual meeting in April 1998. Unisys estimates it will take between three to nine months to find a new CEO.
The Blue Bell, Pa.-based company has hired Spencer Stuart, one of the two executive recruiting firms that conducted International Business Machines Corp.'s CEO search in 1993.
Unisys said it is too early in the process to specify where the company is looking for a successor.
"It's a broad-based, worldwide search that includes people within the company," said Hynes. He declined to comment on whether Unruh's replacement will come from within the computer industry.

Unruh has overseen four restructurings at Unisys. Under his leadership, the company has laid off tens of thousands of employees, closed plants, pared product lines and sold divisions, but has not been able to report consistent revenue growth.

"He has navigated this company through Class 5 rapids and over waterfalls since 1990," Barry Bosak, a Smith Barney analyst, said in a note to clients. "Unruh's decision to step down as chairman/CEO of Unisys is understandable."

The challenge the new CEO of Unisys will face is to find a source of consistent revenue growth within the company, which once relied on mainframe computers. One key growth area, computer services, had some problem accounts and it suffered losses.

"The biggest challenge is to generate consistent revenue growth," said Jay Stevens, an analyst with Buckingham Research Group. "I'm not sure what kind of target a new executive would use, but I'm sure they would like to see something in the low double-digits for revenue growth."
In 1996, Unisys' total revenues were flat, at $6.37 billion, compared with $6.34 billion in 1995. The company also still has a huge debt-to-equity ratio, a hangover from the merger that created it.

"The problem is the legacy that Unruh leaves behind is a debt-to-equity ratio of about 60 percent," said John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst. "The earnings performance is going to be sub-par until they can ... pay off a lot of debt."

Unisys was formed by the 1986 merger of Sperry Corp. and Burroughs Corp. It enjoyed a few years of growth, fueled mainly by cost-cutting, but then entered a prolonged slump as mainframe computers, its chief product, lost favor amid the rise of smaller, cheaper machines.

"(Unruh) did not inherit an easy job from Michael Blumenthal," Stevens said, referring to Unruh's predecessor. "(Blumenthal) may have put together something that had more inherent weaknesses than any realized. Perhaps Unruh feels he has given it his best shot."
Unisys reported a 1997 first-quarter loss equal to 6 cents per share, and a loss for all of 1996 of 41 cents per share.

Analysts declined to speculate on any obvious CEO candidates, except to point out that there are many talented executives at companies like IBM and Hewlett-Packard Co. running business units who might want to run Unisys.

"The new CEO will have to do what Lou Gerstner did," said William Milton, an analyst with Brown Brothers Harriman, referring to International Business Machines Corp.'s CEO. "He will have to spend a lot more time with customers, establishing its identity in markets where it competes with IBM. He will have to shift the company to a growth mode."
Unisys' stock rose 75 cents to $7.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.
